articles.title: NASA Selects Far-Infrared Telescope as First in New Mission Class
articles.description: NASA announced Wednesday a mission to explore the history and evolution of the universe, PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), is advancing to the next phase of development. This space telescope is the first in a new class of NASA astrophysics missions, called Probe Explorers, within the agency’s longstanding Explorers Program. “The PRIMA mission is […]
articles.summary: NASA selects the PRIMA far-infrared telescope as the first mission in a groundbreaking new class designed to explore the universe's history and evolution. This innovative observatory will peer deeper into the cosmos than ever before.

articles.title: BepiColombo begins Mercury arrival with MTM separation success
articles.description: On 3 September 2026 at 15:49 CEST, the European Space Agency's BepiColombo Mission Control Team at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) received the signal they had been waiting for – BepiColombo’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) successfully separated from the spacecraft stack. This landmark achievement for the ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission marks the first step of BepiColombo's long-awaited arrival at Mercury.
articles.summary: BepiColombo successfully completes its Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter separation, marking a major milestone in its historic arrival at Mercury on September 3, 2026. This precision maneuver demonstrates the mission's successful navigation toward its groundbreaking scientific objectives.

articles.title: Astronomers Directly Image the Youngest Exoplanet Ever
articles.description: Most exoplanets we find have been around a long time. They’ve cleared out their orbital path (one of the requirements of planethood, as fans of Pluto well know), have their own gravitational pull, and in many cases shine with their own infrared light. But it takes a long time to get to that point - finding “young” planets is much harder. But a new paper available in The Astrophysical Journal Letters by a research team led by Andrea Bernardi of Diego Portales University in Chile describes a new paper that definitely takes the prize as the youngest exoplanet we’ve yet found.
articles.summary: Astronomers achieve a historic direct imaging of the youngest exoplanet ever discovered, offering unprecedented insights into planetary formation in real-time.

articles.title: JWST finds early galaxies were already seeding the universe with heavy elements
articles.description: When the universe was still in its infancy—only 500 million years after the Big Bang, or about 3% of its current age—some of the universe's earliest stars and galaxies had already formed. Astronomers have long predicted that much of the gas surrounding these young galaxies must have remained relatively pristine, composed mostly of hydrogen and helium, the primordial ingredients available in the newborn cosmos.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope discovers that early galaxies just 500 million years after the Big Bang were already enriching the universe with heavy elements, reshaping models of cosmic evolution.

articles.title: NASA just powered up Roman’s massive 300-megapixel camera
articles.description: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has successfully activated its 300-megapixel infrared camera, which will capture enormous stretches of the cosmos with Hubble-like sharpness. Its planet-hunting coronagraph is also working as expected, putting Roman another major step closer to beginning science operations in 2027.
articles.summary: NASA's Roman Space Telescope successfully powered up its groundbreaking 300-megapixel infrared camera, marking a major milestone toward operation. This will enable unprecedented wide-field observations of the universe.

articles.title: Astronomers Confirm Youngest Known Planet, Less Than 1 Million Years Old
articles.description: Astronomers have confirmed the youngest known planet yet, a Jupiter-size world less than 1 million years old that orbits a star about 450 light-years from Earth, according to a study published Sept. 16 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. The planet, designa…
articles.summary: Astronomers confirmed the youngest known planet ever discovered—a Jupiter-sized world less than 1 million years old still forming in its protoplanetary disk. This exceptional find provides a rare glimpse into planetary formation in real-time.

articles.title: El telescopio espacial Roman ya viaja más allá de la Luna y podría funcionar durante más de 20 años
articles.description: El observatorio Nancy Grace Roman de la NASA avanza hacia el punto de Lagrange L2, situado a unos 1,5 millones de kilómetros de la Tierra. La precisión de su lanzamiento permitió ahorrar tanto combustible que su vida operativa podría superar ampliamente las d…
articles.summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope travels beyond the Moon toward Lagrange Point L2 and is expected to operate for over 20 years, advancing our understanding of the universe.

articles.title: Artemis 2 Set Out to Prove Orion Could Handle Deep Space. Here’s How It Delivered
articles.description: The Artemis 2 mission sent astronauts back to the Moon aboard a spacecraft that had never flown humans before.
articles.summary: The Artemis 2 mission successfully demonstrated that NASA's Orion spacecraft can handle deep space operations while carrying astronauts back to the Moon.

articles.title: Новая статья: Шпионское наследство и триумф баллистики: как телескоп „Нэнси Грейс Роман“ отправился переписывать космологию
articles.description: 30 августа 2026 года со стартового комплекса LC-39A во Флориде была запущена новейшая флагманская обсерватория NASA — Космический телескоп имени Нэнси Грейс Роман NGRST (Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope). Аппарат, чей путь от чертежей до стартового стола зан…
articles.summary: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launches from Florida on August 30, 2026, poised to revolutionize cosmology through its advanced observational capabilities.

articles.title: NASA to Study Human Health, Performance During Crew-13 Mission
articles.description: During NASA’s SpaceX Crew‑13 mission aboard the International Space Station, astronauts will support a series of biomedical and human performance investigations, including a new collaborative effort to study how spaceflight affects blood flow and clotting. NASA also is testing crew members’ manual piloting skills, evaluating methods to counter vision and brain changes, gathering essential health […]
articles.summary: NASA's Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station will conduct comprehensive studies on human health and performance in microgravity. This research is vital for understanding how astronauts adapt to space and informing future long-duration missions.

articles.title: APOD: 2026 September 24 – The Ghosts of Five Supernovas
articles.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 September 24 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss   APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. OriginalAnnotated The Ghosts […]
articles.summary: Today's Astronomy Picture of the Day features the haunting remnants of five supernovas, revealing the spectacular and violent deaths of ancient stars. This celestial image showcases the beautiful aftermath of cosmic explosions captured by advanced telescopes.

articles.title: NASA’s Hubble Telescope Reaches Milestone, Looks for Elusive Supernova
articles.description: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope captured this image of massive galaxy cluster MACS J0417 (left of center) on Sept. 19, 2026. This galaxy cluster acts as a gravitational lens, bending and magnifying light from objects far behind it. Supernova Athena, discovered by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope in 2025, is predicted to reappear between now and […]
articles.summary: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope continues its remarkable legacy by capturing stunning images of massive galaxy cluster MACS J0417 while searching for elusive supernovas. This iconic observatory remains a cornerstone of modern astronomical discovery.

articles.title: Juice to fly past Earth for third gravity assist
articles.description: The European Space Agency’s Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) will return to Earth on 28 September, with flight controllers guiding the spacecraft close to our home planet to alter its speed and direction en route to Jupiter.
articles.summary: The European Space Agency's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) returns to Earth on September 28 for its third gravity assist maneuver. This crucial flyby demonstrates the sophisticated orbital mechanics enabling ambitious deep-space exploration missions.

articles.title: Webb reveals stunning panorama of star formation
articles.description: This starry view of the nearby star-forming region IC 348 is one of the largest images from the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope released to the public so far. Using Webb, astronomers searched IC 348 for brown dwarfs, which are less massive than the smallest stars. The researchers discovered brown dwarfs just twice the mass of Jupiter, bringing the study of these curious objects into a new mass range.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope unveils a stunning panorama of the star-forming region IC 348, one of its largest images to date. This remarkable view reveals the cosmic nursery where stars are actively being born.

articles.title: BepiColombo’s Mercury arrival begins - full replay
articles.description:
Video: 
			02:31:10
				
Watch the replay of the livestream originally broadcast on 3 September as ESA/JAXA's BepiColombo mission took the first critical step towards arriving at Mercury.
After travelling through the inner Solar System together for eight years, BepiColombo's Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) will separate from the rest of the stacked spacecraft on 3 September 2026. This marks the beginning of one of the most complex planetary arrival sequences ever attempted by ESA.
Broadcast live from ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany, the programme includes live views from the iconic Main Control Room, expert analysis, behind-the-scenes insights, and the first signal from the spacecraft following separation. 
Livestream schedule (CEST): 

13:45 – Livestream begins 
16:00-16:45 – End of livestream
articles.summary: BepiColombo's historic Mercury arrival moment is captured in a full livestream replay, allowing space enthusiasts worldwide to witness this momentous achievement. This international collaborative mission marks a triumphant chapter in humanity's exploration of the inner solar system.

articles.title: Hubble's superbubble scene
articles.description:
Image:
			
This sprawling cosmic vista and subject of today’s ESA/Hubble Picture of the Month comes from the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). The LMC is the largest of the small galaxies that orbit our Milky Way galaxy. At just 160 000 light-years away, the LMC offers a close look at highly active stellar birthsites like the nebula shown here. This nebula is named LHA 120-N44, or N44 for short, and it’s located in the constellation Dorado.
The appearance of this photogenic nebula is dominated by two features: a vast central void and a shell of dense, dusty gas. The central void is a ‘superbubble’ spanning roughly 210 by 140 light-years. The glittering stars at the centre of the void are responsible for its creation; through their powerful stellar winds and explosive supernovae, these stars have expelled much of the gas from which they were born.
When the stars of N44’s central star cluster swept away this gas, the expelled gas formed a shell around the superbubble. New stars are forming in this compressed gas shell, making N44 an interesting target for researchers studying the process of star formation. In particular, astronomers have turned to this nebula as an ideal place to time this process from start to finish. Their goal is to understand how long it takes from the collapse of cold gas clouds into dense knots to the moment nuclear fusion ignites in the heart of a newborn star.
Researchers used Hubble to survey N44 and take a census of its stars, cataloguing nearly half a million stars within the cluster as well as interlopers drifting in front of it. Of the stars surveyed, nearly 30 000 are what astronomers call pre-main-sequence stars, which have yet to begin fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores. This treasure trove of baby stars was discoverable thanks to the high sensitivity and fine spatial resolution of Hubble’s instruments that can pick out faint objects in crowded clusters.
The gas shell surrounding the superbubble is energised by ultraviolet radiation from massive stars, causing it to glow and highlighting several distinct features. Each feature within the broader N44 star-forming complex was catalogued by astronomer Karl Henize in the 1950s. One feature is a smaller bubble, catalogued as N44F, that is located near the upper-right corner of this image. N44F is an interstellar bubble blown by the intense stellar winds of a single hot and massive star. As this previously released Hubble closeup shows, the star’s furious winds and radiation have sculpted the surrounding bubble and created pillars of dusty gas.
The data used to create this image come from an observing programme (#14689; PI: Gouliermis) that aimed to probe stars in the N44 complex that have not yet begun fusing hydrogen into heavier elements in their cores. These data help to determine how long the process of star formation takes, as well as what masses newborn stars typically have. Hubble's sensitive observations of the lowest-mass stars in this region open a new window onto star formation in regions that, like the LMC or the galaxies of the early Universe, are poor in elements heavier than helium.
[Image Description: A dense field of stars fills the image, surrounded by wispy clouds of gas and dust. Pale blue and grey nebulosity forms an intricate web across the scene, with darker clouds of dust concentrated towards the lower right. Numerous bright stars appear in shades of blue, white and orange.]
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope captures a stunning cosmic vista of a superbubble structure in the Large Magellanic Cloud, showcasing the dramatic features of stellar regions.

articles.title: Stanford Engineers Teach Spacecraft to "Dream" Their Way to the Space Station
articles.description: Docking with the ISS may seem simple. However, actually doing so is a showcase in how difficult orbital mechanics can be. It’s equivalent to traveling down a highway at 28,000 km/hr and parallel parking into an open garage on a multi-billion dollar laboratory traveling at the same speed. If you try to accelerate forward you actually drift up, and there’s no air friction to naturally slow you down. Oh, and if you hit the lab, everyone onboard both your craft and the station dies, and the resultant debris field could both wipe out dozens of satellites and even people on the ground. No pressure, obviously. For decades, aerospace engineers have been docking successfully using hard coded physics equations and human pilots to correct them. But now, a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from researchers at Stanford, is taking a shot at building an AI to perform a series of “mental simulations” that could fundamentally change how future spacecraft interact with each other.
articles.summary: Stanford engineers develop AI-assisted autonomous docking systems that enable spacecraft to safely navigate the complexities of orbital mechanics when approaching the International Space Station.

articles.title: Strange Galaxies in the Early Universe Were Shaped by Weird Stars
articles.description: Galaxies and their stars in the early Universe look a lot weirder than those we see today, and astronomers want to know why. A team of researchers at the University of Utah decided to survey certain stars in nearby galaxies as analogs of those that existed when the Universe was still in its infancy. The survey, called the "Treasury of Extremely Metal-Poor O Stars (TEMPOS), used the ultraviolet (UV) light streaming from those relatively close-by stars as detected by the Hubble Space Telescope's Cosmic Origins Spectrograph.
articles.summary: Astronomers discover that galaxies and stars in the early universe had distinctly different properties and structures compared to what we observe today, revealing fascinating insights into cosmic evolution.

articles.title: New Lunar Crater Offers Keys To Moon’s Shallow Subsurface
articles.description: Asteroids which strike the Moon and create new craters offer lunar scientists a window onto the workings of our natural satellite’s shallow subsurface.
articles.summary: A newly discovered lunar crater provides scientists with valuable insights into the Moon's shallow subsurface composition and structure through asteroid impact analysis.

articles.title: How Diffractive Solar Sails Could Stop a Killer Asteroid at 100 km/s
articles.description: Asteroids don’t come with a warning label that they might one day hit Earth. While we don’t know of any currently on course to do so, we are finding thousands of new ones each year, and there’s always a potential that one could. We proved a viable technique for dealing with that eventuality - the DART mission successfully moved a small asteroid using a “kinetic impactor” - basically a big rod designed to push the asteroid off its trajectory. But DART had one big flaw - it was traveling in the same direction as the asteroid, and approached it from behind, eventually hitting it with an impactor launched while in orbit around it. That technique might work if we have enough warning, but would require years of orbital mechanical maneuvering to pull off. An alternative, proposed by researchers at Beihang University, is to use a new type of solar sail to deflect a potentially hazardous asteroid by hitting it head on.
articles.summary: Innovative diffractive solar sail technology could provide a groundbreaking method to deflect high-velocity asteroids and protect Earth from potential impacts.

articles.title: Faint young stars reveal spiral galaxy Messier 74 may be twice as large as thought
articles.description: Astronomers have discovered a faint population of young stars extending far beyond the known edge of the nearby spiral galaxy Messier 74. The finding suggests the galaxy is nearly twice as large as previously measured. The new study was published Sept. 4 in Astronomy & Astrophysics.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: A population of faint young stars reveals that the spiral galaxy Messier 74 extends roughly twice as far as previously thought, dramatically revising our understanding of its size.

articles.title: Astrophysicists use wave simulations to open a new window on dark matter
articles.description: Astrophysicists from The University of Hong Kong (HKU), working with a research team led by Beijing Normal University (BNU), have developed a more physically realistic approach to testing how ultralight, or "fuzzy," dark matter could influence gravitationally lensed images. The study is the first to make gravitational-lensing predictions directly from three-dimensional wave simulations of fuzzy dark matter.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astrophysicists employ wave simulations to develop novel observational approaches for understanding dark matter, opening revolutionary new windows into this cosmic mystery.

articles.title: Bennu asteroid samples point to a surprising origin involving Jupiter
articles.description: The asteroid Bennu orbits the sun once every 1.2 years and approaches Earth every six years, passing within around 300,000 kilometers. NASA took advantage of this to collect material from the celestial body. In a spectacular operation in 2023, the US space agency collected samples from the surface of the asteroid Bennu by its OSIRIS-REx probe.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Analysis of samples from NASA's Bennu asteroid mission reveals surprising evidence about the asteroid's origins involving a complex gravitational interaction with Jupiter.

articles.title: NASA's Hubble seeks lensed supernova, marks 200,000 orbits
articles.description: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope completed its 200,000th orbit around Earth on Sept. 19, marking another milestone for an observatory that continues to transform our understanding of the universe.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: NASA's legendary Hubble Space Telescope celebrates a major milestone by completing its 200,000th orbit while continuing to search for rare lensed supernovae.

articles.title: The far side of the moon provides clues to a past magnetic field
articles.description: Unlike Earth, the moon no longer has a core-generated magnetic field. On our planet, the movement of liquid iron in the outer core generates a global magnetic field. This so-called geodynamo works on a similar principle to a bicycle dynamo, which converts mechanical motion into electrical energy. "Today, there is an ongoing heated debate as to whether the moon also operated a dynamo in the past," says Xi Yang, a Ph.D. student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at ETH Zurich. This is because analyses of rock samples brought back to Earth by the Apollo astronauts are contradictory.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Analysis of lunar samples reveals clues about the Moon's ancient magnetic field and how it differs from Earth's current magnetosphere. This discovery helps scientists understand the Moon's geological history and planetary magnetic field generation.

articles.title: “We just need to go back” – Uranus’ moon Ariel may have hidden a 100-mile-deep ocean
articles.description: Ariel, one of Uranus’ moons, may once have contained a subsurface ocean more than 100 miles deep beneath its fractured icy shell. The finding, combined with similar evidence from Miranda, suggests the distant Uranian system could harbor multiple hidden ocean worlds.
articles.summary: Uranus' moon Ariel may have harbored a subsurface ocean over 100 miles deep in its past, suggesting potential for past habitability. This discovery adds Ariel to the growing list of ocean worlds in our solar system worth studying.

articles.title: These massive stars could explain Webb’s strangest galaxies
articles.description: Hubble observations of massive stars in metal-poor dwarf galaxies are revealing clues to why the early universe looks so unusual. Researchers found that stellar winds weaken sharply at extremely low metallicities, potentially allowing massive stars to retain more material and evolve in unexpected ways. The team also found large differences in iron abundance, a key ingredient in stellar winds and supernovae.
articles.summary: Massive stars in metal-poor dwarf galaxies observed by Hubble provide new insights into why the early universe appears surprisingly bright and galaxy-rich. This helps solve a major mystery in cosmology revealed by the James Webb Space Telescope.

articles.title: First stellar stream beyond the Milky Way could reveal dark matter
articles.description: Astronomers have discovered the first globular cluster stellar stream beyond the Milky Way, opening a new way to study dark matter in distant galaxies. These faint trails of stars trace a galaxy’s gravitational structure and could eventually help scientists map invisible matter across the universe.
articles.summary: Discovery of the first globular cluster stellar stream beyond the Milky Way opens a new observational window for studying dark matter. This finding will help astronomers trace dark matter distribution in other galaxies.

articles.title: The Solar System chose fire over ice from the very beginning
articles.description: Ancient iron meteorites reveal that some of the Solar System’s first solid bodies were built mostly from tiny heat-forged rock beads called chondrules, while water-rich dust was largely excluded. The finding pushes this selective planet-building process back to within the Solar System’s first million years.
articles.summary: Ancient iron meteorites reveal that the Solar System's first solid bodies formed primarily from heat-forged material rather than icy components. This discovery reshapes our understanding of planetary formation.

articles.title: Black holes of every size follow the same surprising rule
articles.description: Scientists have found evidence that black holes of vastly different sizes may launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. Supermassive black holes can produce jets soon after tearing apart a star, then fire up again hundreds or thousands of days later when their feeding rate drops to about 2% of the Eddington limit. That same threshold is known to trigger jets from much smaller black holes in the Milky Way.
articles.summary: Scientists discovered that black holes of vastly different sizes follow the same universal rule for launching powerful jets. This finding unifies black hole physics across scales from stellar to supermassive.
